data.question: Should option 1 (block_k 3 → 2), which B and C voted down, be pursued through a regulation-layer override or quorum revision; should option 3 (sanction_lambda 0.5 → 0), a votable compensation step, be adopted; or should the town stay at v1?
data.background: Option 1 passes check and the constitution, and improves on-time deliveries by +7.2 on 5/5 seeds, but B and C voted it down. Adopting it would mean overriding the votes or revising the quorum, which only a human can decide, and in D1 the operator said this belongs to the regulation officer. Option 3 is the votable compensation step D1 asked for, but removing sanctions is a policy choice about deterrence and fairness between companies. It also makes every customer measure worse, so I should not adopt it or reject it on my own.

options.summary: Evict parked robots when 2 robots wait behind instead of 3. On-time deliveries go from 216.6 to 223.8 (+7.2, 5/5 seeds) and late deliveries from 11.4 to 4.2. Blocked seconds fall from 1824 to 936, and the lowest on-time rate rises from 0.93 to 0.97. Road violations rise from 19.0 to 28.0. Votes are A ○, B ×, C ×, so it cannot pass by vote. Adopting it needs a regulation-layer decision (override or quorum revision) by the regulation officer.
options.stakeholders: Customers of all three companies gain: more on-time deliveries, far fewer late ones, and a better on-time rate for the worst-served company. A gains (utility 69.8 → 73.4). B loses (68.5 → 65.5) and C loses heavily (65.8 → 56.3) as the company that parks and blocks most. An override sets a precedent that weakens the companies' veto. Higher road violations may affect road safety and public perception.

options.summary: Remove the overstay sanction multiplier. On-time deliveries fall from 216.6 to 212.2 (-4.4, 0/5 seeds improved) and late deliveries rise from 11.4 to 15.8. Blocked seconds rise from 1824 to 2542, road violations from 19.0 to 36.4, and the lowest on-time rate falls from 0.93 to 0.89. Votes are A ×, B ○, C ○. It does not by itself make option 1 votable; it would only change bargaining positions.
options.stakeholders: C gains most (utility 65.8 → 76.4) and B gains slightly (68.5 → 69.4). A loses (69.8 → 66.4). Customers lose: fewer on-time deliveries, more late ones, and a worse rate for the worst-served company's customers. Deterrence against blocking is removed for every company.

options.summary: Stay at v1: on-time 216.6, late 11.4, blocked seconds 1824, road violations 19.0, lowest on-time rate 0.93. No votes or regulation change are needed.
options.stakeholders: Companies keep their current utilities (69.8 / 68.5 / 65.8). Customers forgo the gains of option 1: about 7 more on-time deliveries and 7 fewer late ones per period. No precedent is set.

recommendation.reason: Option 1 is the only option that improves every KPI measure: the main goal +7.2 on 5/5 seeds, the lowest company on-time rate 0.93 → 0.97, and late deliveries 11.4 → 4.2, with unfinished unchanged at 0. D1 asked for a votable variant first, and the compensation variant (option 3) turned out harmful to customers on every measure (-4.4, 0/5 seeds). It would also only shift utility to C without making option 1 acceptable. Following D1's stated plan, I recommend handing option 1 to the regulation officer as an override or quorum question. The stakeholder effects are explicit: customers and A gain, B loses slightly, C loses about 14% of utility, and road violations rise by 9.0. The operator alone cannot adopt it.
assumptions: The regulation officer is willing to consider an override or quorum revision for this rule change.
Measured results over 5 seeds carry over to real operation in the next period.
The rise in road violations (19.0 → 28.0) does not cross a safety threshold the operator cares about.
B and C will not change their behavior in ways that erase the gains, for example by routing to avoid eviction.

unknowns: sanction_total for each option: the operator required it to be reported (K1), but it is not in this table.
Why B and C vote no: whether it is utility loss alone or concerns about the rise in road violations.
Whether a smaller or targeted compensation (for example a partial sanction change, or a transition-based exemption) could make option 1 votable without harming customers; not measured.
How customers perceive the rise in road violations, and whether it affects safety.
Next period's demand, and whether gains hold under a different load.
How the companies' operating policies would adapt after an override, and whether a precedent would affect future cooperation.
The regulation officer's position on overriding or changing the quorum.
